doc.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995

title: Basie's gestures and compassion; forgotten cymbals at Cohasset
summary: Basie communicated by gesture and hated firing people; Duffy begins his first-night story of leaving cymbals in New York and borrowing Vic Damone's drummer's.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: That’s interesting because a lot of the stories I’ve read about some of the band leaders and especially Basie is that they didn’t always tell you exactly what they wanted in words. It was more with gestures.
And if they didn’t tell you, you were doing okay. And he had a hard time firing people is that right?

Yes, most definitely. It’s very rare that you would be able to upset the Count. He was a very beautiful human being that had a lot of compassion and sensitivity for people. When he had to be total business he knew what to do. Unfortunately when he would receive information that one of the former members had maybe passed away or something like that, and we were in a rehearsal or just getting ready to go on stage or something, he would only give it two seconds thought, “Okay, straight ahead we have to go.” But maybe later on he would have his moment of silence for them. But I learned a lot about the show must go on concept. We were in, let’s see, somewhere in Omaha or something. And we played an engagement there. And we were going to Dallas the next day to play a dance. And one of the gentlemen, Charlie Fowlkes, who played baritone saxophone in the band, he was always dressed to travel every day in a shirt and tie, because of the respect of being seen, you know, he wanted to carry on that tradition of just being classy and being dressed all the time when he was in public. But he was always the first one down in the lobby every day with his luggage, ready to go, you never had to — you might have had to call my room saying, “Duffy, are you ready, the bus is—” you know. I have a very interesting story before I relate that story about Charlie. My first night on the band, we had rehearsed in New York City and I had a brand new set of drums, brand new cymbals, everything. I was ready to go. And so we packed up and we went up to Cohasset, Massachusetts to play at the South Shore Music Circus up there. And we were running a little late in traffic, and we get there with only maybe less than a half hour to set up before we had to play. And the place was packed, ready to go, and there was a theater in the round you know? So I set up my drums, and I said, “Where’s my cymbals?”

Unfortunately my cymbals and my stick bag were left in New York City by accident. And fortunately enough, Vic Damone and a big orchestra, they were rehearsing to open up there the next day, in the little rehearsal room off to the side there. So I ran in and cut off the rehearsal and said, “Excuse me Bas’ I’ll be right with you,” and I went over the Vic’s drummer and I said, you may not know who I am but in around ten minutes I’m going to make my debut with the Count Basie orchestra, and I’m taking your cymbals and your sticks and your brushes, and incidentally what is your name please? I don’t even remember his name.
No, no, but, and I should have had a twenty in my back pocket.
